title: On the Round Complexity of Early Stopping
authors: Wonseok Choi, Wookjin Choi, Xiangyu Liu, and Vassilis Zikas
abstract:
A common pipeline of cryptographic research is: a theory paper asks an interesting question which triggers a line of works; then the problem remains dormant until technology catches up and makes the problem potentially relevant for practice; this triggers a renewed interest which at times pushes the originally theoretical ideas to practice. Several highly influential ideas have followed this pipeline: e.g., the original work on Oblivious RAMs by Goldreich and Ostrovsky [STOC'87\&90],  polynomial commitments by Kate, Zaverucha, and Goldberg [ASIACRYPT'10], and many others. A problem that shows early signs of this pattern is early-stopping Byzantine Agreement (esBA): esBA protocols whose round complexity depends on the number $f$ of {\em actually} faulty parties rather than on (an upper bound on) the number $t$ of {\em potentially} faulty parties. Although it is fair to say that esBA protocols are not (yet) within the practical realm, their potential to improve large scale distributed systems like blockchain ledgers has fueled a number of recent novel results pushing the envelope in esBA feasibility (e.g., Loss and Nielsen [EUROCRYPT'24] and Elsheimy, Loss, and Papamanthou [ASIACRYPT'24]).

    The original starting point of this work has been to advance on the above feasibility questions. But as is common for problems following this trajectory, renewed interest often comes with observations about issues in the assumed definitions and models. Interestingly, our investigation revealed an issue with how the existing literature has been computing the round complexity of such protocols, which yields (previously unobserved) inconsistencies in the  literature of esBA and more generally of synchronous protocols. In a nutshell, the inconsistencies stem from the fact that the last round of several esBA protocols has parties terminating as soon as they send a message to other parties, i.e., they don't need to wait to receive messages sent to them in that round. So, should we count this as an extra round or not? As we observe, different works give different answers to this question, and the answer one adopts affects the claimed tightness of the corresponding bounds.

    Building on the above observation, our work proposes a fine-grained manner of counting synchronous rounds that is both intuitive and resolves these inconsistencies. In a nutshell, our counting distinguishes between rounds in which parties might both send and receive messages, and rounds in which parties only need to send messages. Examining the existing literature through the lens of this round-counting methodology exposes gaps and new open questions in the relevant literature. We resolve these gaps and extend the landscape by several new results.

1   Introduction
The synchronous model of execution is the simplest and most theoretically appealing model for distributed
protocols and cryptographic multi-party protocols. In this model protocols advance in synchronous rounds,
where in each round parties can receive message and act upon message they have seen—e.g., perform some
computation or send messages to other parties. The two most common theoretical instantiations posture
that (1) messages sent in some round are delivered by the beginning of the next round, and (2) messages
sent in some round are delivered by the end of that round. These two instantiations are typically considered
equivalent, as feasibility and asymptotic efficiency questions do not depend on which of the two instantiations
we chose. However, this is not the case for concrete (non-asymptotic) round-complexity results.
    When counting the concrete round complexity of distributed protocols, choosing between the above two
definitions can already create a discrepancy in the calculated round complexity. To see why, consider the
well-known Dolev-Strong Broadcast protocol [DS83], which allows a sender to broadcast his input message
x to a set of n parties, so that every party terminates with an output y satisfying the following properties:
y is the same for all honest (aka uncorrupted or non-Byzantine) parties (consistency), and it equals x (the
sender’s input) if the sender is honest (validity).4 The Dolev-Strong Broadcast protocol tolerates an arbitrary
t < n number of corrupted parties; at a high level, it proceeds in rounds where in each round, every party
pi checks its received messages, and if some message has enough signatures from (a subset of) the n parties
to indicate that it should be included in pi ’s output, then pi includes it, computes a signature to it and
forwards it to the whole party set. The exact details of the predicate that leads to adding the message to
one’s set is not of relevance here; what is important is that in order for the protocol to be secure, the parties
need to compute their output based on messages sent in t + 1 (consecutive) rounds. If fact, as proven already
in [DS83], when considering deterministic and simultaneous termination protocols, the above is a tight bound
on the round complexity.
    The discrepancies introduced by the above two instantiations of the synchronous models are apparent
if one attempts to count the number of rounds for Dolev-Strong: Under the first instantiation, parties need
to wait for round t + 2 to start (so that they receive all messages sent to them in round t + 1) before they
finalize their output and terminate; whereas under the second instantiation, parties receive all the messages
they need by the end of round t + 1 and can immediately terminate. So, should Dolev-Strong be considered
a (t + 1)-round or a (t + 2)-round protocol?
    The above already foggy landscape becomes even more obscure, when considering so-called early-stopping
(synchronous) protocols. In a nutshell, such protocols, aim to relax the connection between round complexity
and (the upper bound on) the number t of corruptions, by making the termination round a function of the
actual number f of faulty parties. (Note that f ≤ t since the adversary might choose to corrupt less than
t parties, or corrupt some parties but still have them run the protocol, i.e., remain non-faulty.) We note in
passing, that such improved round complexity comes at the cost of sacrificing simultaneous termination, i.e.,
different (honest) parties might terminate at different rounds; therefore, in this context, round complexity
counts the number of rounds that the slowest (last) honest party needs to terminate.
    The original starting point of this work was to devise round-optimal early-stopping Byzantine Agree-
ment protocols for various settings (and several of our technical results are attacking this problem). This
endeavor is fueled by an increasingly popular view in distributed systems and blockchain communities that
worst-case corruption models might result in too slow and less scalable protocols in real-world applica-
tions. One way to mitigate such slowdowns is to resort to more restricted adversaries (e.g., only protect
against fail-crashes [FL82,DM86,PR04,PT86] or base security on assumptions about the adversary’s ratio-
nality [GKTZ12]), but discounting on the security end in this way naturally opens up the system to attacks
by stronger adversaries. An alternative approach is to resort to optimistic security with worst-case fallback.
The idea here is for the system to operate in a mode which is highly performant in favorable conditions
(e.g., fast network conditions, perfect synchrony, weaker attackers, etc.) but remains secure (albeit less per-
formant) in worst-case environments. Such optimistic approaches has long been the subject of study in the
cryptographic community [IKK+ 11] and has been recently followed by several real-time distributed systems
and proposals [PS18,BHMN21,CLOZ25]. Early-stopping protocols can be viewed as another instantiation of
this idea: the protocol is secure against t corruptions, but when the number f of actual corrupted parties that
deviate (i.e., faults) is much smaller than t, then the protocol is faster. This is likely the reason that despite
their investigation being mostly dormant since the 90’s, we have recently witnessed a renewed interest in
both cryptography and distributed computing.
    As is natural with problems that stay dormant for long and become popular again due to the demand
for solving them, the early-stopping landscape is fragmented and has several open problems. Interestingly,
however, in the process of solving such open problems, we realized that there is a much deeper issue with the
way the synchronous-protocols literature—even beyond early stopping—has counted rounds that is reflected,
as we will discuss, in inconsistent statements in results published at top venues: In particular, as we shall see

    The above situation has forced us to take a detour from our original technical goal: We first propose a
different way for counting rounds that resolves the inconsistencies in the literature and allows for drawing a
consistent landscape of round complexity for early-stopping Byzantine Agreement (esBA). Armed with this
new notion, we re-evaluate existing literature. Our notion allows us to identify gaps in this literature that
were overlooked due to the ambiguity of the previous round definition(s). This elevated the re-evaluation
to an additional result of its own accord, with several technical contributions, besides the new feasibility
results that we prove here. We view this as evidence both for the need for our more fine-grained definition,
and as an indication that such a definition can be of independent interest for the concrete-round complexity
literature, beyond just early stopping. In the following, we provide an overview of our contributions.


1.1   Overview of Our Contributions

In the following we outline the contributions of our work. We keep the discussion in this section at a relatively
high level, and postpone the exposition of the technical details for our results to Section 2. We include Table 1
that summarizes the landscape of concrete (non-asymptotic) round complexity of esBA and puts our new
results in perspective.


1.1.1 Inconsistencies Resulting from Existing Round-Counting Methods. The starting point of
our work is to revisit constructions and bounds in the classical distributed computing literature that yield
contradictory statements. We note in passing that in this work we use BA to refer to both (Byzantine)
Broadcast (as discussed above) and Consensus, i.e., where instead of a sender only, each of the n parties has
an input and their goal is to agree on the output y (consistency), such that if all (honest) parties have input
x then y = x (validity).
     A classic example of early-stopping BA is the seminal work by Berman and Garay [BG93], which provided
a polynomial-message Consensus protocol tolerating up to t < n/4 corruptions. The number of rounds
claimed this is (at most) min{f + 2, t + 1}. Similarly to Dolev-Strong, the (slowest) parties in [BG93] need
to receive messages sent to them in the min{f + 2, t + 1}-st round to finalize their output. This again
creates an ambiguity depending on whether [BG93] should be considered a min{f + 2, t + 1}-round or an
(min{f + 2, t + 1} + 1)-round protocol, depending on which of the two definitions of synchronous execution
we chose. However, zooming into the protocol from [BG93], one can observe that there are executions where
the slowest party, say p, can compute his output based on the messages sent to it in the first min{f + 2, t + 1}
rounds, but needs to send one more message (a special “done” signal) once he decides to terminate unless
it is already in round t + 1. This “done” message will in-fact not be accounted for by any other party (since
this party is the slowest, hence all other parties can terminate before receiving it); but because p does not
know that he is the slowest one, he has to send that message. (Indeed, eliminating the message altogether
renders the protocol insecure.)
     So now the question becomes: given that everyone (including the slowest party p) will ignore the message
sent by p after round f + 2, shall we consider the above a min{f + 2, t + 1}-round or a min{f + 3, t + 1}-round
protocol?
     By strictly interpreting the description of a round as discussed above, this should be considered as
min{f + 3, t + 1}, no matter which of the two theoretical instantiations we adopt. But one can argue that
this is inaccurate, since everyone by p terminates in round min{f + 2, t + 1} and p himself only needs to send
the message and terminate—i.e., does not need to wait for the round timeout. So, strictly speaking, if a round
lasts τ seconds, considering the above a min{f +3, t+1}-round protocol is badly overestimating the protocol’s
duration. In fact, this latter line of thought is likely the reason why [BG93] claimed the above protocol as
a min{f + 2, t + 1}-round protocol. But the above ambiguity transformed into inconsistencies in follow-up
works, which appear to count such “ignored” send-operation in its round complexity. For example, [GM98]
has a similar terminating-round structure, where the slowest party can compute its output based on the


                                                       3
messages sent to it in the first min{f + 3, t + 1} rounds, but before termination it needs to run two more
rounds to send two more messages; the claimed round complexity in [GM98] is min{f + 5, t + 1} instead of
min{f + 4, t + 1}, which would be inconsistent with the round counting in [BG93]. In a more recent result,
[ELP25] devised a min{f + 3, t + 1} protocol with the above structure, i.e., the last min{f + 3, t + 1}-st
round being an “ignored” send-round by the slowest party. Despite achieving the same round-complexity
as [BG93], which is claimed to be optimal [BG93], this latter result flags itself as suboptimal and posts an
optimal construction as an open problem.
    To summarize, [BG93] and [ELP25] have the same round complexity under the same counting convention
as discussed at the beginning of the introduction, yet one claims to be optimal and the other claims to be
suboptimal. Clearly, only one of them can be right. But which one?
    As we shall show, the answer to the above is itself obfuscated by the existing vague round counting
methodology. In particular, the answer depends on whether or not the corresponding lower bounds render
the last (send-only) rounds as necessary. As it turns out, the existing lower bound [DRS90], which uses fail-
crashes only, does not render this round necessary. In fact, the lower bound does not require parties to wait
to receive their f + 2-round message. So does this mean that the above protocols are not round-optimal? Not
necessarily! Since the lower bound holds for crash failures, it may be too loose to prove tightness for protocols
tolerating Byzantine faults. A reader familiar with such round-complexity lower bounds of distributed fault-
tolerant protocols might assume this is not the case, as most such tight bounds are in fact proven for weaker
corruption/fault types and then matched by a protocol. Notwithstanding, in what we consider a surprising
result, we are able to prove that considering Byzantine corruptions does add (at least) an extra receive-only
round to the lower bound.

1.1.2 A Consistent Methodology for Counting (and Comparing) Rounds of Synchronous Pro-
tocols. A core thesis of our work is that the above ambiguity in claims is a result of a round-counting
methodology, which is inadequate for crisply capturing the round-optimal esBA landscape. In order to untie
the above Gordian knot, and devise a proper language that allows for a clear classification of different esBA
protocols, we propose a fine-grained round-counting methodology, which explicitly disambiguates rounds in
which parties need to send messages and still wait to receive messages sent to them from rounds in which
they simply send messages and terminate. In a nutshell, every round is split into two mini-rounds: in the first
mini-round, the party sends a message and might perform some computation on its local state; in the second
mini-round, each party receives all messages sent to it in the first mini-round and updates its local state
accordingly. When mapping this model to a real-world implementation of synchrony, the network latency
(aka timeout) ∆ is the time that passes between the first and second mini-rounds.
    We refer to rounds in which a party needs to process both the first and the second mini-rounds as
send/receive rounds (or, simply, receive rounds) and denote a protocol that requires t such rounds as a
t(r)-round protocol. We refer to a round in which the protocol only executes the first mini-round (and then
terminates) as a send(-only) round, and denote a protocol that requires t − 1 send/receive rounds and an
additional send-only round as a t(s)-round protocol. Given the above round-counting methodology, it is
straightforward to classify the aforementioned results: [BG93] and [ELP25] are min{f + 3(s), t + 1(r)}-round
Consensus and Broadcast protocols, respectively, tolerating Byzantine parties. On the other hand, [PR04] and
[PT86] are min{f +2(r), t+1(r)}-round Consensus and Broadcast protocols, respectively, tolerating omission
faults. The known lower bound for BA [DRS90] assumes fail-crashes and requires at least min{f +2(s), t+1(r)}
rounds.

1.1.3 Revisiting and Charting the Feasibility Landscape. Armed with such an accurate methodol-
ogy for counting rounds, we can now investigate the gaps in the literature.

esBA in the Presence of Omission Faults. The first gap is with respect to omission corruptions. Recall
that the existing lower bound is for fail-crashes and mandates min{f + 2(s), t + 1(r)} rounds. However, to
our knowledge, the best known construction tolerating omission faults is by Perry and Tueg [PT86] and
is a min{f + 2(r), t + 1(r)}-round Broadcast protocol (i.e., in case f < t − 1, the protocol from [PT86]


                                                       4
needs an additional receive mini-round which in terms of time incurs an extra latency ∆ delay). We close
this gap by constructing the first min{f + 2(s), t + 1(r)}-round Broadcast protocol tolerating any t < n
omission-corrupted parties. (We note in passing that our protocol follows the classical definition in [PT86]
for Broadcast in the presence of omission failures, where parties output either a value or ⊥.) By having
every party broadcast his value in parallel and then adopt a value if it appears on the output more than n/2
times (otherwise output ⊥) this also yields the first min{f + 2(s), t + 1(r)}-round Consensus protocol against
omission-corrupted minorities. We note in passing that the min{f + 2(r), t + 1(r)}-round protocol in [PR04]
was designed for the so called uniform Consensus problem (see Section B.3). Since this is a stronger variant
of Consensus, it is conceivable that the lower bound is also tighter.

Tighter Lower Bounds. As discussed, the existing min{f + 2(s), t + 1(r)} lower bound (proven for crash
faults) [DRS90] is not sufficient for proving tightness of the various existing esBA constructions that pro-
vide min{f + 2(r), t + 1(r)}-round BA protocols [BGP92,ZIP95] or min{f + 3(s), t + 1(r)}-round protocols
[BG93,MW94,ELP25]. Filling in this gap we prove that min{f + 2(r), t + 1(r)} rounds are necessary for esBA
tolerating Byzantine corruptions, thereby strengthening the lower bound of [DRS90] and establishing the
optimality of [BGP92,ZIP95]. We further prove that for Broadcast tolerating dishonest (Byzantine) majori-
ties, an extra send round is necessary, making min{f + 3(s), t + 1(r)} the lower bound for this case. Albeit
existing min{f + 3(s), t + 1(r)}-round protocols are for honest (super-)majorities, as such their optimality
remains an open question [BG93,MW94,ELP25].

Revisiting the EIG-based esBA Protocol [BG93]. Exponential Information Gathering (in short EIG)
was introduce in the seminal paper of Lamport, Shostak, and Pease [LSP82] that introduced the problem
of BA and gave first solution. Albeit, as the name suggests, EIG is an exponential space/time protocol—it
effectively consists of multiple rounds in which the players relay all the information they have received to
everyone, and then attempt to achieve a consistent decision (see Section 3.2 for details).
    Similarly to the classical BA literature, where the first protocol was exponential (in the player set size n)
time/space and was later on improved to polynomial (in fact, linear) [GM98], esBA experienced a similar tra-
jectory. The first optimally resilient (tolerating up to t < n/3 corruptions) protocol was exponential [BGP92]
and was in-fact relying on EIG. The follow-up work by Berman and Garay [BG93] achieved polynomial (in
n) complexity by lowering the corruption tolerance to t < n/4. As discussed above, the work achieved (in our
terminology) a min{f + 3(s), t + 1(r)}-round protocol. The high-level idea of [BG93] is to alternate between
phases that use an EIG-style protocol for a few (constantly many) rounds, and phases where parties use
smart voting to compress their state so that it remains polynomial. A similar approach was more recently
taken by Abraham and Dolev [AD15] to provide an optimally-resilient (i.e., t < n/3) with a similar early
stopping-bounds as [BG93].
    Re-examining these results under the spectrum of our fine-grained round-counting exposes counter-
intuitive results: As discussed, the lower bound we could prove for BA is min{f + 2(r), t + 1(r)} rounds
(which is different from the min{f + 3(s), t + 1(r)}-round protocol of [BG93]). Notwithstanding we were able
to revise the protocol of [BG93] so that it does not need to send the extra “done” message in the last (send-
only) round. This modification requires non-trivial white-box surgery to the original protocol as outlined in
Section 2.4. As we prove, the revised protocol does achieve the min{f + 2(r), t + 1(r)} bound which we prove
optimal for t < n/4 Byzantine corruptions, restoring the optimality claim of [BG93].

A New Optimally Resilient Tight-Rounds Early-Stopping BA Protocol. Last but not least, we turn
to the question of round-optimal and optimally-resilient esBA assuming a (signatures) setup. Here, Elsheimy,
Loss, and Papamanthou [ELP25] recently provided an exponential early-stopping Broadcast protocol that
makes use of ideal signatures, tolerates up to t < n/2 corruptions and terminates in min{f + 3(s), t + 1(r)}
rounds. Recall that since we are in the t < n/2 realm, this trivially implies an exponential early-stopping
Consensus protocol (for the bound t < n/2 which is optimal for Consensus) by having every party broadcast
their input in parallel and take the majority of the outputs. However, as the authors observe, the protocol
is not tight given the state-of-the-art lower bound min{f + 2(s), t + 1(r)} from [DRS90] (for crash faults).
In fact, even given our newly proven lower bounds of min{f + 2(r), t + 1(r)} for Byzantine corruptions


                                                       5
(Theorem 2), there remains a gap. As our last (and most) technical contribution, we devise a new exponential
min{f + 2(r), t + 1(r)}-round protocol. Our protocol follows a very different approach than that of [ELP25]
and both the construction and proof are technically challenging.
    In addition to the non-trivial contribution, our protocol replaces the assumption of ideal signatures with
that of a setup for information-theoretic signatures [HSZI00,SHZI02]. The reason for this choice is that the
use of ideal signatures within an exponential-time protocol has attracted criticism from the cryptographic
community as an overly abstract hybrid assumption: how can we choose the parameters so that no adversary
polynomial in them can forge signatures of honest signers? Instead, in this work we use the concrete construc-
tion of information-theoretic, in-short i.t. (pseudo-)signatures from [IOZ14]. Such i.t. pseudo-signatures are
setup hungry primitives (i.e., they assume a correlated-randomness setup which is polynomial to the longest
message to be signed) but provably achieve unforgeability against unbounded adversaries as long as they are
not transferred to too many different users. As such, although in the abstract protocol design one can treat
them like an information-theoretic analog of existentially-unforgeable signatures [GMR88], their concrete
invocation requires careful choice of the setup size and extra care so that they are not reused (even verified)
more than their allowed number of times. To keep the protocol description modular, in Section 8 where we
provide our optimal esBA construction and proof intuition, we ideally treat them as existentially-unforgeable
signatures. A discussion of how to instantiate them with i.t. signatures (and in particular how to chose the
parameters) so that the way they are used in the protocol does not compromise their security guarantees is
given in Appendix A.

2    Technical Overview

2.1   Receive-Round f + 2 Lower Bound for Byzantine Faults

The f + 2 lower bound for BA protocols was first established by Dolev, Reischuk, and Strong [DRS90]. In
fact, from the arguments in [DRS90,AS24], it is only guaranteed that if an honest party p is allowed to
terminate in round f + 1, then there exists another honest party q that eventually terminates with a distinct
value, thereby violating consistency. Furthermore, the lower bound proof assumes the weakest adversaries,
i.e., assumes only crash faults. Under our refined notion of rounds, this result implies an f + 2(s) lower
bound against crash faults. Yet, since all existing BA tolerating Byzantine faults require at least f + 2(r),
this naturally raises the question of the tight (lower) bound for Byzantine faults:
   What is the exact lower bound for BA protocols in the Byzantine fault model? Does there exist an optimal
protocol that attains it?
     We prove the f + 2(r) lower bound for Byzantine faults, thereby completing the f + 2(s) lower bound
for crashed faults by [DRS90]. To understand the high-level intuition, we first recall the (restated) proof
by Abraham and Stern [AS24] for crash faults. Since the protocol satisfies validity, there must be a crucial
party p∗ such that—fixing the inputs of all other parties—changing the input of p∗ , and hence its first-round
message, can alter the decision value of an honest party. If p∗ crashes after sending its message to some party
pi , then from pi ’s view no faulty behavior is detected and pi will terminate with some value v. However,
other honest parties may delay their termination since a failure of p∗ is detected, and their final decision
may differ from v given that p∗ is crucial. The same reasoning applies inductively through round f + 1: if
one crash-faulty party is detected per round from 1 to f , then no honest party pif can safely terminate in
round f + 1 when no crash fault is detected. This leads to the f + 2(s) lower bound.
     In the Byzantine fault setting, the crucial party p∗ is more subtle since it can send conflicting messages
to different honest parties. Specifically, p∗ can send message m to honest party pi in some round, inducing
pi to terminate with value v, while simultaneously sending a conflicting message m′ to another honest party
pj and inducing pj to terminate with v ′ ̸= v. Since p∗ appears honest from the views of both pi and pj ,
allowing them to terminate in this round—where no Byzantine behavior (including the crash fault) has
been detected—would violate consistency. Therefore, honest parties must wait for one additional round of
messages before termination, yielding the f + 2(r) lower bound as claimed.

2.3   f + 2(s) Broadcast Protocol Tolerating Omission Faults

While we have proven that f + 2(r) are necessary for BA against Byzantine faults, it leaves another open
question on the tightness of BAs against crash and omission faults. Is f +2(r) necessary or f +2(s) sufficient?
It is somewhat surprising that, to the best of our knowledge, there is no known tight BA protocol tolerating
crash or omission faults but existing ones require f + 2(r) [PT86,PR04]. Hence, we fill the gap by providing
a simple but elegant Broadcast protocol for any t < n, achieving min{f + 2(s), t + 1(r)} round termination.
The protocol utilizes two special symbols, Null and ⊥, to propagate any important misbehavior it observes
in a certain round. Since there is no Byzantine behavior (but only crash and omission faults), once a party
received a value v ∈ D, which is not Null nor ⊥, it can echo the value and terminate. The core problem
is how to determine the safe condition to terminate with ⊥, which implies that one can be sure that no
other party terminates with another value. To help this decision, a party sends Null to others once it has not
received any echoes of v ∈ D in a certain round. The Null messages constitutes the fact that the sender (of
Null messages) is still honest to the receiver, although the sender could not receive any v ∈ D yet. Once the
number of parties that have sent Null is larger than n − r + 1, the protocol guarantees that there will be no
one terminating with a value other than ⊥.


2.4   Revisiting BG93

We observe that Cloture Vote protocol in [BG93] requires min{f + 3(s), t + 1(r)} in our round counting
model, since a party is required to send “I am done” after it outputs a value in (at most) round f + 2(r). At
a high level, the consistency of the Debate protocol relies on Liveness: if an honest party p resolves a node
σ in round r, then all other honest parties must also resolve σ consistently by round r + 1. Here σ = p1 ...pℓ
denotes a sequence of (non-repeating) parties indexing a node in the EIG tree structure (see Section 3). To
achieve this property, p must send messages in round r + 1, though this requirement is not explicitly stated
in [BG93]. Again, in the worst case, honest parties may decide their output value in some Debate protocol
in round f + 2, which forces them to send the corresponding messages in round f + 3 even though no honest
party needs to receive them.
    We propose a revised version of [BG93] that reduces the round complexity to min{f +2(r), t+1(r)} by the
following modifications. First, we switch the meaning of 1 and 0 for ‘cloture’ in the invocation of the Debate
protocol. In the Cloture Votes protocol in [BG93], the “I am done” message from p is indeed unnecessary, as it
merely indicates that p will vote ‘Continuation’ permanently. If silence is simply interpreted as ‘Continuation’
at the beginning of each Debate, then the “I am done” message becomes redundant. Therefore, in our revised
Cloture Votes protocol (Fig. 8), we redefine 0 to represent ‘Continuation’ and 1 to represent ‘Cloture’, since
the default value for silence in Debate is 0. Second, we introduce a new rule for handling silence in the Debate
protocol: If no message is received from σx, then the value of σx is assumed to be the same as that of σ. This
rule effectively ensures Liveness although there is no message from honest parties that have already resolved
the node in the previous round. Naturally, no party can resolve a node before Debate starts. Therefore, if
the first message in Debate is missed, then it is replaced by 0, consistent with the rule above. With this
modification, honest parties no longer need to send messages about nodes resolved in the current round. In
addition, we present more detailed proofs and specification of the early-stopping variant in [BG93] to help
readers better understand this seminal work.

2.5   Early-Stopping Broadcast for t < n/2

The construction of f + 2(r)-round early-stopping Broadcast is challenging. Toward this, an honest party
p must terminate in some round r that appears to be round f + 2 from p’s perspective. However, r may
not actually be the round f + 2, as Byzantine parties can deceive p into believing that r = f + 2. Once
p terminates, it can no longer send information, and all other honest parties must still terminate with a
decision value consistent with p. If t is sufficiently small, Byzantine parties must involve a large number of
honest parties to deceive p into believing that r = f + 2. In this case, the remaining honest parties can
easily infer and follow p’s decision value without further communication from p. However, when t is large,
the problem becomes significantly more difficult. In such cases, the other honest parties must treat p’s silence
itself as a source of information.
    [BGP92] is the first protocol to demonstrate how to exploit silence to achieve early stopping by round
f + 2. The silence of p indicates that p has already resolved the ancestor node and therefore requires no
further information about that branch. (If the ancestor node is the root, this means that p has terminated.)
Thus, silence must not be treated as the receipt of a default message, since it conveys the information about
the specific value p has resolved. This idea is further simplified in [AD15]: If no message is received from p
regarding σ, the value from σ is used instead of a default value. Using this approach, [BGP92] and [AD15]
achieve early stopping by round f + 2 under the condition t < n/3.
    When t ≥ n/3, Byzantine Broadcast protocols additionally rely on signatures for authenticity: Every
message sent by a party is accompanied by a signature, allowing others to publicly verify its origin. Moreover,
the message itself may include all messages and signatures from previous rounds, forming a signature chain
that possibly originated from the designated sender. However, this situation makes another challenge to
achieve early stopping by round f + 2. As discussed above, if a party p does not send a message with respect
to a node in the EIG tree, then it indicates that p has already resolved an ancestor node of it. However,
this also breaks the continuity of the signature chain. Namely, if silence represents that an ancestor node
is resolved, then a party q must not remain silent when q fails to receive a message from p; otherwise,
q’silence would incorrectly suggest that it has resolved an ancestor node, when in fact it has not. At the
same time, q cannot produce a valid message continuing from p, due to the lack of the valid signature from
p. To address this, q must instead generate a special message indicating ‘I did not receive a message from
p’. In our protocol, we denote this with the symbol Null. Nevertheless, it is possible that a Byzantine party
x generates a Null message and q fails to receive that message. In this case, q must generate Null message to
indicate that it did not receive x’s message. Importantly, q’s Null message is not an echo of x’s message, and
the two messages are distinguished. Hence, it is crucial that a Null message explicitly specifies who missed
whose message.
    Our protocol allows parties to start new signature chains dynamically during execution. In the traditional
EIG Broadcast protocol with signatures, only the signature chain initiated by the sender in round 1 is
considered valid [DS83,ELP25]. In contrast, our protocol permits the signature chain of a Null message to
be initiated by any party in any round. This capability ensures that honest parties can correctly convey
information about who missed whose message. The intuitive description of the protocol is described in
Section 8.3.

3.1    Problem Setting and Assumptions
Network and Synchronous Model. We consider a fully connected network of n parties P executing a protocol
in a synchronous setting. All parties share a global clock, and there exists a known upper bound ∆ on the
message delay between honest parties. This assumption allows each protocol execution to proceed in discrete
rounds of length ∆, where every message sent by an honest party at the beginning of round r is guaranteed
to be delivered to all honest parties by the end of that round (or, by the beginning of round r + 1).
    Following the structure required for our analysis, we further refine each round into two mini-rounds: a
send (mini-)round and a receive (mini-)round. Note that this decomposition is purely syntactic and does not
modify the underlying synchrony assumption or the known delay bound ∆. We discuss the new model in
more details in Section 4. From here, we always consider the round model in which each round starts with
the send-round, and all messages sent in round r are received by round r.

Adversarial Model. We assume an adversary (either probabilistic polynomial-time (PPT) or computationally
unbounded) that can adaptively corrupt up to t parties, where t can be varied with respect to the protocols
we will discuss. Once corrupted, a party is under full control of the adversary and may deviate arbitrarily
from the prescribed protocol, including sending inconsistent or forged messages. The adversary can choose
which parties to corrupt during the execution, based on the entire protocol transcript observed so far. Unless
otherwise specified, an adversary is rushing—it can observe all messages sent by honest parties within a
round before determining the messages of corrupted parties for the same round.
   All honest parties are assumed to know the parameters (n, t, ∆) in advance and to have authenticated
point-to-point channels between every pair of parties.

Signatures. In Section 8 we utilize (digital) signatures [GMR88] to ensure authenticity, non-repudiation, and
transferability. To better focus on the protocol and proofs, we skip the setup of the signature scheme, and
simply assume all parties have access to ideal signing and verification in a black-box way with the following
properties:
 – Correctness: Signatures generated by honest parties always verify.
 – Unforgeabilty: Except with negligible probability,5 no adversary can generate a valid signature of an
   honest party on a fresh message.
 – Consistency: Except with negligible probability, no adversary can create a signature that verifies differ-
   ently for two (honest) parties.
    We emphasize that our construction requires information-theoretic signatures [HSZI00,SHZI02,SS11], i.e.,
the above properties hold even against computationally unbounded adversaries. This requirement stems from
that a party (no matter honest or Byzantine) is assumed to run in exponential time, since the message size
(and thus the signing and verification time) increases exponentially with n. To maintain security in this
setting, we resort to the information-theoretic signatures, albeit at the cost of an exponentially expensive
setup phase. In Appendix A, we provide the formal definitions of information-theoretic signatures along with
a detailed asymptotic complexity analysis of our protocol in Section 8.

     Although the EIG protocol achieves BA, it suffers from a significant drawback: exponential message
complexity O(nt ) and exponential running time. Consequently, considerable effort has been devoted to
improving its complexity. A key observation is that a party p can often determine the value of RT p (σ) in
the EIG protocol before round t + 1. Once p fixes the resolved value of σ, it can stop gathering information
about the entire subtree of IT p rooted at σ, hence reducing the message complexity. This phenomenon is
commonly referred to as fixing or prediction [MW94,BG93,GM98].
     In the original EIG protocol, nodes are resolved at the end of execution based on the values contained
in RT . However, nodes can instead be resolved earlier during the execution using the values contained in
either IT or RT . We classify resolve rules based on IT as IT resolve rules, and those based on RT as RT
resolve rules. The details of resolve rules depend on the specific protocol.
     Another important technique is fault masking. During protocol execution, a Byzantine party q may
attempt to prevent nodes from being resolved by, for example, sending inconsistent messages. However,
such behavior also provides evidence that q is Byzantine. Once q is detected as Byzantine, honest parties
can simply ignore the messages from it. One particularly simple form of fault masking is to treat a party
detected as Byzantine as sending a fixed value (e.g., 0) for all nodes of interest. Therefore, if all honest
parties recognize that q is Byzantine (we refer to this state as globally detected ), it is equivalent to as-
suming that q sends the same message to all honest parties, implying that q can no longer disrupt the
agreement process. This technique has been utilized in various works to reduce the message complexity
[DRS90,BNDDS92,MW94,BG93,GM98,AD15].
     In spite of these techniques, EIG methods still suffer from exponential message complexity. Several EIG
protocols [BG93,GM98,AD15] employ a mechanisms known as the monitor vote to attain polynomial message
complexity. The monitor vote process serves as a mechanism to ensure the safe abort of the EIG protocol
when the data size of honest parties becomes excessively large. This concept was first introduced by Berman
and Garay [BG93], under the name Cloture Votes protocol.
     [BG93] first introduced the Debate protocol, an EIG-based protocol with a round complexity of min{f +
2, t + 1} and resilience up to t < n/4.8 However, the Debate protocol suffers from exponential message
complexity. To achieve a polynomial message complexity, the Cloture Vote protocol recursively invokes the
Debate protocol in each round. These subprotocols (Debate protocols) are identical to the Debate protocol
invoked in round 1, except that each is initiated in a later round, with the parties’ inputs initialized to a
special symbol ‘Continuation’. More precisely, if the data size of an honest party p becomes excessively large,
i.e., beyond a predefined threshold, then p votes for ‘Cloture’; otherwise, it votes for ‘Continuation’ in that
round.
     Since the Debate protocol itself is an early-stopping BA protocol, it can be used to reach a consistent
decision on whether to cloture, thereby ensuring agreement among all honest parties. Furthermore, the
Debate protocol guarantees that at least one Byzantine party is excluded from the protocol in each round
(otherwise, it terminates within a constant number of rounds). As a result, when a subprotocol is invoked
in round r, at least r − 1 Byzantine parties have already been excluded from that Debate. Therefore, the
Debate protocol invoked in round r can also terminate by round min{f + 2, t + 1}, even though it starts in
round r.
     The protocol proposed by Abraham and Dolev in [AD15] has a similar structure to that of [BG93]. They
first introduce an EIG subprotocol (like the Debate protocol in [BG93] but without a designated name), which
achieves BA with a round complexity of min{f + 2, t + 1} and resilience up to t < n/3, but suffers from
exponential message complexity. To obtain polynomial message complexity, the Monitor Vote protocol (the
main protocol) repeatedly invokes the EIG subprotocol in each round. However, the difference in resilience
required a much more complicated and sophisticated approach.

5     Revisiting the Lower Bounds

In this section, we revisit the f + 2 lower bound for crash faults in [DRS90], and provide two tighter lower
bounds, i.e., the min{f + 2(r), t + 1(r)} lower bound for Byzantine faults and the min{f + 3(s), t + 1(r)} lower
bound for Broadcast with dishonest majority, under our refined model in Section 4.


5.1   f + 2(r) Lower Bound for Byzantine Faults

Dolev, Reischuk, and Raymond [DRS90] proved the f + 2 lower bound—more precisely, f + 2(s) lower
bound—for (eventual) BA protocols. In this section, we follow the proof by Abraham and Stern [AS24] for
crash faults, and devise a new impossibility result, i.e., the f + 2(r) lower bound, for BA protocols with
Byzantine faults distinguished from those for crash faults.


                                                           16
    Recall that for the crash fault, the (faulty) party will either send an honest message, uniquely determined
by the protocol with respect to each receiver, or crash, i.e., it will send no message at all. However, faulty
parties with Byzantine behaviors can send conflicting messages to different parties. If there exist multiple
different faulty behaviors, the protocol may terminate with different outputs for each behavior. This is a
crucial distinction when we first try to prove an impossibility result for Byzantine faults instead of crash
faults. However, we will show that crash fault behavior is sufficient to generate critical configuration, and
only one Byzantine behavior in critical round is enough to result in inconsistency: There is at most one
faulty party per round, and the faulty party follows the protocol description, except in the following cases:
1) it may crash; and 2) when generating a message to send, it may compute the message as if it had not
received a message from the previous faulty party. This limited behavior is sufficient to induce inconsistency
by round f + 1.
    If a party sends conflicting messages to honest parties, then the honest parties may detect the faulty
behavior and ignore the faulty party in subsequent rounds. Building on this observation, to prove Theorem 2,
we assume that the Byzantine party crashes at the end of the round in which it behaves in a Byzantine
manner. This assumption simplifies our analysis without affecting the tightness of the bound.
    In later rounds, the adversarial strategy can be more complex, but somewhat surprisingly, our simplifi-
cation can show a tight bound for some cases, which implies that the behavior we described is indeed the
best strategy for adversaries in some cases. For warm-up, we start by showing that f + 2(r) are necessary
for BA, where we will consider only two possible messages for each Byzantine faults.

7.1      Review of the Cloture Votes Protocol
Cloture is a parliamentary procedure (aka “parliamentary guillotine”) to curtail unnecessary long debates.
In the Cloture Votes protocol [BG93], the unanimous will of the honest parties (akin to a parliamentary
supermajority) may curtail the debate if they are required to send a big message over the pre-set threshold.
This is facilitated by having the parties initiate a new so-called Debate protocol (see Fig. 5) in each round,
which either ends quickly, with the conclusion “continue” or “terminate with the default value”, or lasts
through many rounds. By repeatably invoking Debate, the Cloture Votes protocol solves the Consensus
problem with message complexity O(n5 ) in the setting n > 4t.

The Debate Protocol. The Debate protocol (Fig. 5) extends the basic EIG protocol by additionally introducing
fault masking and early stopping. Namely, if an honest party p detects q as Byzantine, then all (·, q, ·) entries
in IN rq→p are replaced with the default value v0 , i.e., (·, q, v0 ). Moreover, if in round r the value of some
node σ has been fixed (or predicted) by all honest parties, then all σ-projections are unnecessary to send,
making these branches stop early. Consequently, the Debate protocol has much shorter messages compared
with the original EIG protocol.
    We defined reliable node σp as in Definition 3. Note that in EIG trees, there are also nodes where σ
includes some honest parties. Nevertheless, [BG93] protocol guarantees that all honest parties resolve the
consistent value of a reliable node σp in round |σp| + 1. Once the consistent value of an ancestor node was
resolved, the values of its descendant nodes become irrelevant, as they do not affect the final output of the
protocol. Therefore, we only need to consider reliable nodes and unreliable nodes.
    As mentioned above, the consistent value of a reliable node σq must be resolved in round |σq| + 1 in the
protocol. Consequently, if a node σq is not resolved by that round, then q must be a Byzantine party.
Definition 9 ((Fully/Partially) Corrupted Nodes in [BG93]). A node σq that has not been resolved
by round |σq| + 1 (by some party p) is called a corrupted node (with respect to p).
    Moreover, at the end of round |σq| + 1, if no honest party resolves σq, then it is called a fully corrupted
node; if some honest parties resolve σq while others do not, then it is called a partially corrupted node.
    Furthermore, if σq is a fully corrupted node, we say that q fully corrupts σq. If σq is a partially corrupted
node, we say that q partially corrupts the node σq.
    The protocol is designed such that if an honest party p resolves a node σq in round r, then all other
honest parties will consistently resolve σq in round r + 1, i.e., in the next round. This implies that, to prevent
the protocol from terminating in the next round, at least one of Byzantine parties must fully corrupt a node
in each round. Otherwise, all honest parties will resolve all unresolved nodes at the current level, causing
the protocol to terminate. However, if a Byzantine party q fully corrupts a node in round r, then all honest
parties will detect q as a Byzantine party in round r + 1, since any reliable node must be resolved by that
round. Once a Byzantine party q is globally detected, the protocol ensures that q can no longer corrupt a
nodes by fault masking, effectively excluding q from the agreement process. Therefore, Byzantine parties can
continue to disrupt the agreement process only until round min{f + 2, t + 1}, as at least one Byzantine party
must be excluded in each round.
    When the Debate protocol is invoked in the Cloture Votes protocol in round r, there are at least r − 1
Byzantine parties that have been detected and hence the messages from them are replaced with the default
value. This guarantees that in the worst case, an invocation of the Debate subprotocol in round r will last
for at most t − r + 2 rounds,14 and hence terminate in round t + 1.
    The Debate protocol itself suffers from exponential message complexity at the adversary’s will. If Byzan-
tine parties continue to disrupt the agreement process until round min{f + 2, t + 1}, then at most one fully
corrupted node can exist in each round, resulting in a message complexity of O(n2 ). However, suppose that
j Byzantine parties fully corrupt nodes as many as possible in each round. In this scenario, the Byzantine
parties can sustain this behavior up to ⌊f /j⌋ rounds, resulting in a total of j ⌊f /j⌋ fully corrupted nodes.
This expression is maximized when j = e, but since j must be the natural number, the maximum occurs at
j = 3. Consequently, the worst-case message complexity of the protocol becomes O(3f /3 ) = O(3n/12 ).

7.3   Revised Cloture Votes: An f + 2(r) Consensus Protocol

We now present the revised Cloture Votes protocol. We start by observing several points of the original
description that merit refinement. In [BG93], the protocol was designed to run t + 1 rounds and was later
adapted to support f + 2 early stopping. However, this adaption is incomplete and introduces inconsistencies
in the description. For example, in Debatekp , party p must send a message once after determining the output
of Debatekp to ensure consistency under early stopping. Since the original protocol was structured to continue
round t+1, this requirement was omitted. Moreover, [BG93] provides only a brief outline of the early-stopping
variant without full pseudocode, leaving some operational details to be inferred.
    While the protocol in [BG93] is secure, the proof as presented misses some steps in detail. Specifically,
Lemma 3.1 in [BG93] only addresses the case where |Fp | + 1 < r, leaving open the possibility that another
honest party q could terminate inconsistently after round r. In our revised version, we provide a proof that
covers all cases and demonstrate that the revised protocol is a Byzantine Consensus protocol guaranteeing
termination by min{f + 2(r), t + 1(r)}.
    In our revision, we first switch the meaning of 1 and 0 for ‘Cloture’ in the invocation of the Debate protocol.
In the Cloture Votes protocol in [BG93], the “I am done” message from p is indeed unnecessary, as it merely
indicates that p will vote ‘Continuation’ permanently. If silence is simply interpreted as ‘Continuation’ at
the beginning of each Debate, then the “I am done” message becomes redundant. Therefore, in our revised
Cloture Votes protocol (Fig. 8), we redefine Debate(0) to represent ‘Continuation’ and Debate(1) to represent

Key Technique 2: Beyond Liveness: Early Stopping via Persistency. Most existing early-stopping
EIG-based BA protocols aim to achieve a property known as Liveness. Liveness means that if an honest
party p resolves a node σ in round r, then all other honest parties also resolve σ consistently within a
constant number of rounds. By Liveness, once p resolves σ, it can immediately close σ and no longer needs
to consider it. This key property enables early stopping in EIG protocols: if p resolves the root, it can
terminate immediately. Although not always explicitly stated, most early-stopping EIG protocols satisfy
Liveness [MW94,BG93,ZIP95,GM98,AD15]. However, when n ≤ 3t, Liveness becomes extremely challenging,
although we believe that both early stopping by f + 2(r) and Liveness can still be achieved simultaneously
under 2t < n ≤ 3t. Interestingly, if signatures are available, early stopping can be achieved without Liveness.
Instead, we introduce Persistency: if an honest party p resolves a node σ in round r, then all other honest
parties also resolve σ consistently during their output decision process.
    To achieve Persistency, our output decision algorithm becomes more complex than any other existing
protocols achieving Liveness. When every node at level r has a resolved ancestor or is itself resolved by p in
round r (Line 18 in Figure 11), p applies the output decision algorithm.
    If the root node (s) is already resolved, p outputs the value of RT p (s) (Line 2 in Figure 12). Otherwise,
there exists a node σ that is itself unresolved but all of whose child nodes are resolved by p. For such a node,
if p can apply RT Resolve Rule, then p resolves σ via RT Resolve Rule (Line 6 in Figure 12). If p cannot apply
RT Resolve Rule, then p proceeds to the next step.
    If there exist two child nodes resolved with (v, k) and (v ′ , k ′ ), respectively, where (v, k) ̸= (v ′ , k ′ ) and
k, k ′ ≤ |σ|, then p resolves σ with RT p (σ) = (Null, |σ| + 1) (Line 9 in Figure 12). This condition implies that
the party q with σ = σ ′ q has signed two conflicting messages. Furthermore, it is guaranteed that no honest
party resolves σ before the output decision process (see Lemma 32 and Theorem 9 for details). Therefore,
p nullifies σ by resolving it with (Null, |σ| + 1). Note that no node σ can be resolved with (v, k) such that
k ≥ |σ| + 2. Consequently, if σ is resolved with (Null, |σ| + 1), this node cannot affect the resolved value of
its parent node, which corresponds to the neutralization of σ.
    Otherwise, there are two cases. If there exists a child node resolved with (v, k) where k ≤ |σ|, then p
resolves σ with RT p (σ) = (v, k) (Line 11 in Figure 12). This condition implies that at least one honest party
received a message containing ⟨σ ′ , q, (v, k)⟩ from q with σ = σ ′ q. Therefore, p resolves σ with RT p (σ) = (v, k),
since it is possible that some honest party has already resolved σ with (v, k). If there is no child node resolved
with (v, k) where k ≤ |σ|, then p resolves σ with RT p (σ) = (Null, |σ|+1) (Line 13 in Figure 12). This condition
implies that no honest party received a message containing ⟨σ ′ , q, (v, k)⟩ from q with σ = σ ′ q. Therefore, p
nullifies σ with RT p (σ) = (Null, |σ| + 1), since no honest party resolved σ before the output decision process.
    With this output decision algorithm, the protocol can achieve Persistency (Theorem 9). Consequently,
if some honest party resolves a node σ, then every honest party resolves σ consistently. If no honest party
resolves a node σ, then every honest party can resolve σ consistently, since the output decision algorithm
resolves σ based on the resolved values of its child nodes, which are themselves resolved consistently. During
the output decision process, every honest party resolves the unresolved nodes from the deepest ones up to
the root node. Finally, every honest party resolves the root node consistently, and RT (s) is the output value
of the protocol (Line 14 in Figure 12).

9    Conclusion
We introduce a new fine-grained notion of round, which consists of a send-(mini)-round and a receive-(mini)-
round, for consistent counting of round complexity (Section 4). Based on this fine-grained round, we find
that the known lower bound for the round complexity of BA against crash faults is in fact f + 2(s) while all
existing BAs against Byzantine faults are required to have at least f + 2(r) rounds. Thus, we newly prove
that the lower bound for the round complexity of BA against Byzantine faults is f + 2(r) (Section 5).
    This leaves an open question about the tightness of BA against crash and omission faults. Is f + 2(r)
necessary, or is f + 2(s) sufficient? To answer this question, we provide a new Broadcast protocol for any
t < n, achieving min{f + 2(s), t + 1(r)} round complexity against omission faults (Section 6). Thus, we show
that f + 2(s) is the tight round complexity against crash or omission faults.
    Furthermore, we prove that if t > n/2 and f is sufficiently small, then BA requires at least f + 3(s)
(Section 5). This result implies that f + 3(s) may be the tight round complexity for BA in the dishonest-
majority setting, although we fail to prove it for large f . This again leaves an open question about the
tightness of BA. Is f + 2(r) the tight round complexity for t < n/2? A BA protocol achieving f + 2(r) round
complexity for t < n/3 is already known [BGP92]. However, for t ≥ n/3, such a protocol is unknown. We
provide a new elegant protocol achieving f + 2(r) round complexity for t < n/2 (Section 8). Thus, we prove
that f + 2(r) is the tight round complexity for t < n/2, while f + 3(s) may be the tight round complexity
for t > n/2.
    Some protocols [BG93,MW94] claimed to achieve optimal round complexity (f + 2), but their actual
round complexity is f + 3(s). This difference is nontrivial. We demonstrate a revision of [BG93] that fixes
its round complexity from f + 3(s) to f + 2(r) (Section 7). This revision involves several nontrivial changes
to the protocol.
    Open questions:
1. What is the lower bound of round complexity for t = n/2?
2. Is f + 3(s) the tight round complexity for t > n/2?

B     Additional Related Works
In this section, we provide additional related works of BA in general, including (im)possibilities and protocols
in various models.

B.1    Feasibilities and Impossibilities
The Byzantine Agreement (BA) problem, also known as the Byzantine General problem, is one of the
fundamental problems in distributed computing since it was first introduced in [PSL80,LSP82]. These works
showed that, if n denotes the total number of parties and t denotes the maximum number of faulty parties,
then n > 3t is necessary for solving BA. One way to circumvent this limitation is to assume an unforgeable
signature scheme [GMR88]. Under this assumption, Dolev and Strong [DS83] showed that BA can be solved
for any t < n.
    It is also known that, when n and t are the number of entire parties and the maximum number (threshold)
of faulty parties, Fischer and Lynch [FL82] proved that at least t + 1 synchronous communication rounds are
necessary to solve the BA problem deterministically. On the other hand, Ben-Or [Ben83] and Rabin [Rab83]
showed that randomized BAs can circumvent the lower bound. If the network is asynchronous, the celebrated
result of Fischer, Lynch, and Paterson [FLP85] proved that solving deterministic BA is impossible even in the
presence of only one faulty processor. Garay et al. [GKKO07] pushed the feasibility boundary of randomized
BAs up to t = n/2 + O(1). They also established an asymptotically matching lower bound, proving that no
randomized BA can terminate in fewer than 2n/(n − t) − 1 rounds whenever n − t ≥ 2. Lindell, Lysyanskaya,
and Rabin [LLR02] showed that, while authenticated BA protocols can be secure for t < n, they require
t < n/3 to remain secure under parallel or concurrent composition.

B.2    Randomized BAs (with Honest Majority)
One of the first notable works in this regime is Feldman and Micali [FM88], who proposed BA protocols
achieving expected constant-round complexity. They considered both synchronous and asynchronous net-
works, and also both information-theoretic and cryptographic settings. Indeed, randomized BAs can be


                                                         57
classified into those two types: BAs that assume cryptographic primitives—and therefore secure against
only computationally bounded adversaries—and BAs that are information-theoretically secure. The line of
research [CR93,ADH08,PCR14,CFG+ 23] studied asynchronous BAs in the information-theoretic setting. In
the synchronous model, Goldreich and Petrank [GP90] presented a method to eliminate a failure probability,
achieving expected constant-round complexity and worst-case round complexity of O(t) for t < n/2. Zam-
sky [Zam96] achieved an expected constant-round complexity and the optimal worst-case complexity of t + 1
rounds for a resilience of t < n/8. Achieving 1) expected constant round complexity, 2) t + 1 rounds worst
case, and 3) optimal resilience t < n/3 altogether is still an open problem.
    In the cryptographic setting, Katz and Koo [KK06] and Abraham et al. [ADD+ 19] proposed BA pro-
tocols achieving t < n/2 and expected constant-round complexity. For the dishonest majority, Fitzi and
Nielsen [FN09] proposed randomized protocols with expected round complexity O(k) when t = n/2 + k.
Chan, Pass, and Shi [CPS20] proposed a sublinear-round BA, and Wan et al. [WXSD20] extended the
feasibility of expected constant-round Broadcast to tolerate any constant fraction of corruptions.


B.3      Early-Stopping BAs
Dolev, Reischuk, and Strong [DRS90] studied early-stopping protocols to achieve the BA problem, dubbed
eventual BA in their work. They proved that, when f is the actual number of faulty parties, deterministic
BA protocols should run at least min{t + 1, f + 2} communication rounds in a synchronous network. They
also provided a round-optimal early-stopping BA protocol requiring n > max{4t, 2t2 − 2t + 2}. Since then,
various researchers have sought to find more efficient early-stopping BA protocols. The first known early-
stopping BA achieving both optimal round complexity and resilience (i.e., t < n/3) is [BGP92], at the cost
of exponential message complexity. The line of research [BGP92,BG93,MW94,ZIP95,GM98,PR04,AD15]
has tried to improve and balance between the three quantities: round complexity, message complexity, and
resilience. Parvédy and Raynal [PR04] claimed an optimal BA protocol but only tolerating omission faults.16
    The recent breakthrough to achieve early-stopping BA for t < n was made by Loss and Nielsen [LN24] by
proposing a new primitive, dubbed ‘polariser’, based on a signature scheme. The polariser allows parties to
accuse faulty parties and provide evidence, eventually lets honest parties exclude faulty parties that disturb
the termination within O(f ) rounds per each such faulty party. This ultimately leads to a Broadcast protocol
that achieves O(min{f 2 , t}) round complexity. Later, Deligios, Klasovita, and Liu-Zhang [DKLZ25] fine-
tuned the polariser by carefully dealing with the structure of the communication graph and consequently
achieved O(f )-round BA for t < (1 − ϵ)n for any constant ϵ > 0. Both protocols, however, are far from
optimal in terms of round complexity. Another approach to close the gap was taken by Elsheimy, Loss, and
Papamanthou [ELP24]. They provided an early-stopping Consensus protocol for t < n/2 and any (pre-fixed)
positive integer d, and it terminates in (d+5)·(⌊f /d⌋+2)+2 rounds. Later, the same
                                                                                √ authors [ELP25] proposed
another protocol by removing the need for a constant d, and achieved f + 6⌈ f ⌉ + 6 round complexity. In
the same work, the authors also introduced a nearly optimal early-stopping Broadcast protocol for t < n/2
that terminates in min{f + 3, t + 1} rounds with exponential message complexity, while the protocol only
requires sending a message (but no receiving) in the final round, which turns out to be the major issue of
our work.


B.4      BAs in Other Fault Models
Groce et al. [GKTZ12] considered game-theoretic adversaries, i.e., rational adversaries. They showed that
perfectly secure BA is possible for t < n when the adversary’s preferences are given. Zikas, Hauser, and
Maurer [ZHM09] considered the mixed fault model with Byzantine omission faults. In this line of research,
Eldefrawy, Loss, and Terner [ELT22] showed a lower bound in this model, and Loss and Stern [LS23] showed
a matching protocol.
